structure.title: Chapter I · State the boundary
structure.text: Mill asks when society may compel an individual. Public opinion joins law in the dock, since a neighbour who fears losing work and friendship can feel a threat even where Parliament has forbidden nothing.

structure.title: Chapters II–III · Give dissent somewhere to live
structure.text: Suppressing a belief can bury a truth. Mill presses further by considering what happens to a true belief whose adherents never hear an objection. Individual experiments in conduct extend the argument from what people may say to how they may live.

structure.title: Chapters IV–V · Try the principle on difficult neighbours
structure.text: Drink, trade, dangerous goods and family obligations test the proposed boundary. Mill repeatedly changes one circumstance to show how conduct that concerns the agent in one setting can expose another person to injury in the next.

people.name: Harm
people.text: Disliking a person's conduct and identifying an interest it injures are different acts of judgment. Mill's examples make the distinction harder as soon as another person relies on the agent to fulfil a definite obligation.

people.name: Custom
people.role: An authority nobody had to elect
people.text: People can imitate the available pattern so thoroughly that they hardly develop preferences of their own. Mill's defence of eccentricity concerns the capacity that withers when imitation supplies every choice in advance.

context.title: The audience of the principle
context.text: Mill limits his argument to people he regards as capable of mature deliberation and notoriously excludes societies he depicts as undeveloped. The exclusions matter when assessing the reach of the universal-sounding language he uses elsewhere.

notice.text: Follow the corn dealer from print to his own doorstep.
notice.why: Mill changes the circumstances in which an accusation is uttered, placing an excited crowd outside a particular man's house. The sentence can stay the same while its relationship to an impending harm changes.

notice.text: Look at the believer who has won every argument by default.
notice.why: An inherited truth can become a formula its defenders cannot explain. Mill counts the loss of understanding as a cost of silencing the opposition even when the opposition is mistaken.

opening: A whole society agrees that an opinion is dangerous, foolish, or disgusting. John Stuart Mill asks what gives it the right to silence the person who holds it. His defence of liberty extends beyond unpopular speech to unpopular ways of living, where neighbours can enforce conformity without ever calling the police. The argument becomes most demanding when tolerance costs something: when the person being protected seems wrong, the experiment looks reckless, and everyone respectable would feel more comfortable if it stopped.
